definitions.l3: A sentence that is either true or false. Questions and commands are not statements.
definitions.l4: A sentence with a definite truth value: either true or false. Even if you don't know which it is, it is still a statement.
definitions.l7: A declarative sentence that is either true or false; commands, questions, and expressions without a verb are not statements.

definitions.l3: An if–then claim. It promises that whenever the 'if' part holds, the 'then' part holds too.
definitions.l4: A statement of the form 'if p then q', written p ⇒ q. It is false only when p is true and q is false.
definitions.l7: A statement 'p ⇒ q' that is false in exactly one case: p true and q false. This convention makes the conditional true whenever the hypothesis fails — so-called vacuous truth.

definitions.l3: The 'if' part of an if–then claim. It is what you get to assume when proving the claim.
definitions.l4: The 'if' clause of a conditional p ⇒ q; the assumption you're allowed to make.
definitions.l7: The antecedent of a conditional statement — the assumed condition from which the conclusion is to be derived.

definitions.l3: The 'then' part of an if–then claim. It is what you must show.
definitions.l4: The 'then' clause of a conditional; what the claim promises.
definitions.l7: The consequent of a conditional statement — the claim that must follow from the hypothesis.

definitions.l4: A conditional p ⇒ q is vacuously true when the hypothesis p is false — no promise is broken because the case never arose.
definitions.l7: A universal or conditional claim is vacuously true when the domain of the claim is empty or the hypothesis never holds, so there is nothing to check.

definitions.l3: The opposite of a statement. Its truth value is flipped.
definitions.l4: For a statement p, the negation ¬p is true exactly when p is false.
definitions.l7: The logical operation ¬ that maps a statement to the statement with the opposite truth value.

definitions.l3: One example that shows a rule is wrong.
definitions.l4: A single instance where a universal claim fails; enough to disprove the claim.
definitions.l7: An element of the domain of a universally quantified statement that falsifies the statement.

definitions.l4: A well-defined collection of objects; membership is either true or false, and order and repetition do not matter.
definitions.l7: A well-defined collection of objects. Well-definedness means that for every object, it is unambiguously either in the collection or not.

definitions.l3: A set whose every element is also in another set.
definitions.l4: A ⊆ S when every element of A is an element of S.
definitions.l7: For sets A and S, A ⊆ S means ∀x (x ∈ A ⇒ x ∈ S).

definitions.l3: A rule that gives every input exactly one output.
definitions.l4: A rule f: S → T that sends each element of S to exactly one element of T.
definitions.l7: A function f: S → T is a rule assigning to each s ∈ S a unique f(s) ∈ T. Equivalently, a subset of S × T meeting the totality and single-valuedness conditions.

definitions.l4: A function is injective if different inputs give different outputs.
definitions.l7: f is injective (or one-to-one) if f(x₁) = f(x₂) implies x₁ = x₂.

definitions.l4: A function is surjective if every element of the codomain is actually hit.
definitions.l7: f: S → T is surjective (or onto) if for every t ∈ T there exists s ∈ S with f(s) = t.

definitions.l3: A perfect pairing: every input goes to its own output and every output is hit exactly once.
definitions.l4: A function that is both injective and surjective.
definitions.l7: A function that is both injective and surjective, equivalently a function with an inverse.

definitions.l3: A rule we agree on before any proofs, so that the proofs have somewhere to start.
definitions.l4: A statement accepted as true without proof. Everything else is proved from the axioms.
definitions.l7: A statement of a mathematical theory taken as true without proof, forming the base from which theorems are derived.

definitions.l3: A number is even if it can be shared into two equal groups — that is, if it is 2 times some whole number.
definitions.l4: An integer n is even iff n = 2k for some integer k.
definitions.l7: An integer n is even iff n = 2k for some k ∈ ℤ.

definitions.l3: A number is odd if sharing it into two groups leaves one left over.
definitions.l4: An integer n is odd iff n = 2k + 1 for some integer k.
definitions.l7: An integer n is odd iff n = 2k + 1 for some k ∈ ℤ.

definitions.l3: We say m divides n (written m | n) if n is m times some whole number.
definitions.l4: For integers m, n, we write m | n when there exists k ∈ ℤ with n = mk.
definitions.l7: For m, n ∈ ℤ, m | n means ∃k ∈ ℤ with n = mk. Divisibility is an existence statement.

definitions.l3: A real number that cannot be written as a fraction of two whole numbers.
definitions.l4: A real number that is not in ℚ.
definitions.l7: A real number x for which no p, q ∈ ℤ with q ≠ 0 satisfy x = p/q.

definitions.l3: A way to prove a statement for every counting number at once, by starting at 0 and stepping up one at a time.
definitions.l4: A proof method: verify the base case A(n₀), then prove A(k) ⇒ A(k+1) for all k ≥ n₀; conclude A(n) for all n ≥ n₀.
definitions.l7: The principle: for any predicate A on integers ≥ n₀, if A(n₀) holds and ∀k ≥ n₀ (A(k) ⇒ A(k+1)), then ∀n ≥ n₀ A(n).

definitions.l3: The successor of a number is the number that comes right after it.
definitions.l4: The successor of x ∈ ℕ, written S(x), is 'the next natural number' — the operation we use to define addition.
definitions.l7: The function S: ℕ → ℕ postulated by Peano to be injective, whose image excludes 0.
